citation: Heller, J. I., Shinohara, M., Miratrix, L., Rabe Hesketh, S., & Daehler, K. R. (2010). Learning Science for Teaching: Effects of Professional Development on Elementary Teachers, Classrooms, and Students. Paper presented at the Society for Research on Educational Effectiveness (SREE) Conference, 2010. (ERIC document ED514193). NSF-funded study conducted by WestEd / Heller Research Associates.
report_number: ERIC ED514193 (2010 SREE Conference paper; NSF-funded). Peer-reviewed journal version: Heller, Daehler, Wong, Shinohara & Miratrix (2012), J. Research in Science Teaching, 49(3), 333-362, doi:10.1002/tea.21004.
design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial; unit of assignment = teacher/class (teachers randomly assigned within site and within school to four conditions: three PD course models + one no-treatment control). 8 national research sites, 54 districts in six states. 268 fourth-grade teachers (teaching electric circuits) with complete pre/post data; ~5,280 students (Table 3) with student content-test data. Subject = elementary science (electric circuits unit); grades = grade 4 (registry codes 3-6). Three PD arms: A=Teaching Cases, B=Looking at Student Work, C=Content Immersion (called Metacognitive Analysis in the 2012 journal version); D=Control. Impact estimates from hierarchical linear models (3 levels: PD course, teacher, student) on student gain scores (post minus pre percent correct), adjusting for pretest via gain outcome plus site/round/experience covariates. Only one of the three PD arms maps to registry row 45 conceptually (single 'TPD for curricula' arm vs business-as-usual); all three TPD-vs-control contrasts are extracted and tagged row_id 45 so the central merge can select/average as appropriate.
problems: Source is a brief SREE conference paper (the 2010 version the meta-analysis cited), not the fuller 2012 JRST article, so reporting is condensed. (1) The three PD course models all share identical science content and differ only in pedagogy-analysis features; they were each contrasted against the SAME no-treatment control, so there are three TPD-vs-control student-achievement effect sizes, all extracted under registry row 45 (which the registry lists as a single-arm 'TPD for curricula' RCT). The central merge may need to pick one arm or average across arms to avoid double-counting the shared control; flagged here. (2) Outcome is a researcher/developer-made test of electric-circuits content knowledge administered as pre/post (gain score) -- NOT a standardized independent test -- so these would likely be filtered centrally (the meta-analysis used independent measures); extracted and labeled test_type=researcher_made per spec. (3) The reported effect sizes (0.39, 0.52, 0.52) are computed by the authors as HLM treatment coefficient / pooled SD of student gain. The standardizing SD is not printed explicitly; it was reverse-engineered as the overall pooled SD of student gain across all four groups from Table 8 = 14.53 (sqrt of n-1 weighted pooled gain variance of the four arms), which reproduces all three reported ES exactly (5.7/14.53=0.392->0.39; 7.5/14.53=0.516->0.52). (4) Impact estimate SEs (1.4, 1.4, 1.5) are from the HLM Table 10, so clustering is already accounted for (cluster_adjusted=true); g_se = J*(SE/standardizing SD). (5) ICC is NOT reported as a design-effect ICC; the value recorded (~0.168, teacher-level) is DERIVED from the Table 10 random-effects SDs (SD teacher=5.9, SD residual=13.1, SD course=1.1) for information only and was not used in computing g (which is already cluster-adjusted). (6) n_clusters per contrast = arm teachers + control teachers (Table 3: A=70, B=65, C=54, control=79). Per-arm student n from Table 8 (analytic gain-score samples; total 5,246, slightly below the 5,280 with any content-test data in Table 3); control n=1494.

effect_sizes.arm_label: Course A: Teaching Cases (science PD) vs no-treatment control
effect_sizes.test_name: Student test of electric-circuits science content knowledge (developer-made, percent correct), gain score (post minus pre)
effect_sizes.timepoint: post (within two weeks after the electric circuits unit, 2007-08; gain = post minus pre)
effect_sizes.g_method: d = HLM treatment coefficient / standardizing SD = 5.7 / 14.5307 = 0.39227, where 14.5307 = overall pooled SD of student gain across all four groups (Table 8: sqrt of n-1 weighted pooled gain variance), which is the 'pooled standard deviation of student gain' the authors used (reproduces reported ES 0.39 exactly). Hedges' g = J*d, df = n_t+n_c-2 = 2839, J = 1 - 3/(4*df-1) = 0.999736, g = 0.39217. g_se = J*(impact_se/standardizing SD) = 0.999736*(1.4/14.5307) = 0.09632; g_var = g_se^2 = 0.009278.
